questions.title: Query Optimization with EXPLAIN ANALYZE
questions.question: How do you identify and fix slow database queries?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **`EXPLAIN ANALYZE`: actual execution plan with row counts and timing**
- **Seq Scan on large table = missing index or bad query structure**
- **SELECT *: fetch unnecessary columns → avoid, especially with JOINS**
- **Pagination: use cursor/keyset instead of OFFSET on large datasets**
- **N+1 queries: load 100 orders, then 100 user queries = 101 queries**
- **Slow query log: identify queries taking > 100ms automatically**

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Query optimization starts with identifying slow queries — either via application monitoring (Micrometer recording query times), the database's slow query log, or `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` directly. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` runs the actual query and shows the execution plan with real row counts and timing at each step.

The most common culprits are: missing indexes causing sequential scans on large tables, SELECT * fetching unnecessary data, N+1 queries from lazy-loading ORM relationships, and OFFSET-based pagination that requires the database to scan and discard thousands of rows.

Fix strategies: add appropriate indexes for WHERE and JOIN columns, select only the columns you need, use JOIN FETCH or EntityGraph to avoid N+1, and switch to cursor/keyset pagination for large datasets.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## EXPLAIN ANALYZE — Reading the Output

```sql
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT o.id, o.total, u.email
FROM orders o
JOIN users u ON o.user_id = u.id
WHERE o.status = 'PENDING'
  AND o.created_at > '2024-01-01'
ORDER BY o.created_at DESC
LIMIT 20;

-- OUTPUT (PostgreSQL):
-- Limit  (cost=1234.56..1234.89 rows=20 width=48) (actual time=245.3..245.6 rows=20 loops=1)
--   -> Sort  (cost=1234.56..1289.45 rows=21955 width=48) (actual time=245.2..245.3 rows=20)
--         Sort Key: o.created_at DESC
--         Sort Method: top-N heapsort  Memory: 27kB
--       -> Hash Join  (cost=892.30..1155.12 rows=21955) (actual time=8.3..240.1 rows=21955)
--             Hash Cond: (o.user_id = u.id)
--             -> Seq Scan on orders o  (cost=0.00..245.00 rows=21955) ← PROBLEM!
--                   Filter: ((status='PENDING') AND (created_at > '2024-01-01'))
--                   Rows Removed by Filter: 28045
--             -> Hash  (cost=512.00..512.00 rows=12000)
--                   -> Seq Scan on users u

-- DIAGNOSIS:
-- Seq Scan on orders → full table scan (10M rows)
-- actual time: 245ms → needs optimization
-- Both orders and users doing Seq Scan

-- FIX:
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_status_created ON orders(status, created_at DESC);
CREATE INDEX idx_users_id ON users(id);  -- PK should already have this

-- AFTER INDEX:
-- Index Scan on orders  (actual time=0.05..1.2 rows=21955 loops=1)
-- actual time: 1.4ms  ← 175× improvement
```

## Common Query Anti-patterns

```sql
-- ANTI-PATTERN 1: SELECT * (fetches unneeded columns)
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42;
-- If orders has 30 columns including blob columns (attachments, descriptions)
-- Even if you only use 3 fields — you fetch all 30

-- FIX: Select only needed columns
SELECT id, status, total, created_at FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42;

-- ANTI-PATTERN 2: OFFSET pagination (must scan and skip rows)
SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY created_at DESC OFFSET 50000 LIMIT 20;
-- DB must read 50,020 rows and discard first 50,000 → gets SLOWER as page increases

-- FIX: Keyset/cursor pagination
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE created_at < :lastSeenCreatedAt  -- 'cursor' from previous page
   OR (created_at = :lastSeenCreatedAt AND id < :lastSeenId)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20;
-- Always reads exactly 20 rows, regardless of 'page number'

-- ANTI-PATTERN 3: Functions on indexed columns destroy index usage
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2024;  -- MySQL
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE DATE_TRUNC('year', created_at) = '2024-01-01'; -- PostgreSQL
-- Even with index on created_at, function prevents index use

-- FIX: Use range condition instead
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE created_at >= '2024-01-01' AND created_at < '2025-01-01';
-- Index on created_at CAN be used now

-- ANTI-PATTERN 4: OR across different columns prevents single index use
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42 OR email = 'x@y.com';

-- FIX: UNION ALL with separate indexes
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42
UNION ALL
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE email = 'x@y.com' AND user_id != 42;
```

## N+1 Query Problem and Fix

```java
// N+1 PROBLEM:
List<Order> orders = orderRepository.findByStatus(PENDING);  // 1 query
for (Order order : orders) {
    String email = order.getUser().getEmail();  // N queries (1 per order)
    // If user is LAZY-loaded, this fires a separate SELECT per order
}
// 100 orders = 101 SQL queries total

// FIX 1: JOIN FETCH in JPQL
@Query("SELECT o FROM Order o JOIN FETCH o.user WHERE o.status = :status")
List<Order> findByStatusWithUser(@Param("status") OrderStatus status);
// 1 query with JOIN: SELECT o.*, u.* FROM orders o JOIN users u ON o.user_id = u.id

// FIX 2: @EntityGraph
@EntityGraph(attributePaths = {"user", "items", "items.product"})
List<Order> findByStatus(OrderStatus status);
// Spring Data builds the JOIN FETCH automatically

// FIX 3: DTO projection (best for performance — fetch only needed fields)
@Query("SELECT new com.example.dto.OrderSummary(o.id, o.total, u.email) "
     + "FROM Order o JOIN o.user u WHERE o.status = :status")
List<OrderSummary> findSummariesByStatus(@Param("status") OrderStatus status);
// Selects only 3 columns, 1 query, no entity hydration overhead
```

## Slow Query Detection

```sql
-- PostgreSQL: Enable slow query logging
-- postgresql.conf:
-- log_min_duration_statement = 100  -- Log all queries > 100ms
-- log_statement = 'all'  -- Log ALL statements (development only)

-- Find slowest queries via pg_stat_statements:
SELECT query, calls, mean_exec_time, total_exec_time, rows
FROM pg_stat_statements
ORDER BY mean_exec_time DESC
LIMIT 20;

-- MySQL: Slow query log
SET GLOBAL slow_query_log = 'ON';
SET GLOBAL long_query_time = 0.1;  -- Log queries > 100ms
SET GLOBAL slow_query_log_file = '/var/log/mysql/slow.log';

-- Spring Boot: Log Hibernate SQL with timing
logging:
  level:
    org.hibernate.SQL: DEBUG
    org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.bind: TRACE
    org.hibernate.stat: DEBUG

spring:
  jpa:
    properties:
      hibernate:
        generate_statistics: true  # Log stats per query
```

## Production Reality

Set up the slow query log from day one — it's invaluable for catching regressions before users complain. In Spring Boot, enable Hibernate statistics in staging to see query counts per request; an endpoint that fires 200 queries is a N+1 problem waiting to hurt you in production. Use `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` in PostgreSQL for full analysis including buffer cache hits — this tells you if the problem is I/O or CPU.
